abstract: Early life adversity (ELA) creates lasting impacts on the brain and behavior that contribute to vulnerability for psychiatric disorders. Most rodent models of ELA involve manipulating maternal care itself (e.g., maternal separation) or involve changes to the environment that alter maternal care (e.g., low resources). Here, we used neonatal predator odor exposure (POE) as a threat model of ELA in rats where pups themselves are exposed to stressful odors in the absence of the dam. Our previous research shows that POE results in long-term behavioral effects, including reduced social play, but we have yet to determine whether POE also alters maternal care in ways that could contribute to these outcomes. To investigate this, litters were removed from their home cage and exposed to either POE or control conditions from postnatal days 1-3. Immediately following this exposure, pups were returned to their home cage and placed on the side opposite of the nest. Retrieval of pups to the nest and maternal care behaviors were recorded for 45 minutes. On nearly all measures there were no differences in maternal behaviors between POE and control dams. Some behaviors changed across days similarly in POE and control groups: time spent licking and grooming pups increased, and time spent nest building and rearing decreased across days. The only significant difference between conditions was observed on day 1, with control dams spending more time carrying pups during retrieval but this decreased to POE levels on days 2 and 3. Ultimately, maternal care behavior remains largely unchanged by POE. These findings provide evidence that long-lasting effects of POE on offspring are due to POE itself, and not due to changes in maternal care behavior.
